title: CPR
summary: CPR (cardiopulmonary resuscitation) helps keep blood flowing to the brain and organs when someone's heart has stopped.
steps: Check the scene is safe, then check for responsiveness by tapping and shouting.
Call emergency services or ask someone nearby to call immediately.
Lay the person flat on their back on a firm surface.
Place the heel of one hand on the center of the chest, other hand on top, and push hard and fast at about 100-120 compressions per minute.
Allow the chest to fully rise between compressions.
Continue compressions until emergency responders arrive or the person shows signs of life.
If trained, give rescue breaths after every 30 compressions.

title: Choking
summary: Choking occurs when the airway is blocked, and quick action can help clear it before breathing stops.
steps: Ask the person if they are choking; if they can cough or speak, encourage them to keep coughing.
If they cannot breathe, speak, or cough, call emergency services right away.
Stand behind the person and lean them slightly forward.
Give 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand.
If that doesn't work, give 5 abdominal thrusts (Heimlich maneuver) above the navel.
Alternate back blows and abdominal thrusts until the object is dislodged or help arrives.
If the person becomes unresponsive, begin CPR and continue until help arrives.

title: Burns
summary: Prompt cooling and protection of a burn can reduce damage and pain while waiting for further care.
steps: Remove the person from the source of the burn to stop further injury.
Cool the burn under cool (not ice-cold) running water for 10-20 minutes.
Gently remove any tight clothing or jewelry near the burn before it swells.
Cover the burn loosely with a clean, non-fluffy cloth or sterile dressing.
Do not apply ice, butter, or ointments to the burn.
For large, deep, or facial/genital burns, call emergency services immediately.
Watch for signs of shock and keep the person warm and calm.

title: Wound Care
summary: Basic wound care focuses on stopping bleeding and preventing infection until proper treatment is available.
steps: Wash your hands or wear gloves before touching the wound if possible.
Apply firm, direct pressure to the wound with a clean cloth or dressing.
Elevate the injured area above heart level if it does not worsen the injury.
Once bleeding slows, clean gently around the wound with clean water.
Cover the wound with a sterile bandage or dressing.
Seek medical attention for deep, large, or heavily bleeding wounds.
Watch for signs of infection such as redness, swelling, or fever in the following days.

title: Seizure
summary: During a seizure, the goal is to protect the person from injury and stay calm until it passes.
steps: Stay calm and time the seizure from start to finish.
Clear the area of hard or sharp objects to prevent injury.
Place something soft under the person's head if possible.
Do not hold the person down or put anything in their mouth.
Gently turn the person onto their side once shaking stops to keep the airway clear.
Stay with them until they are fully alert and oriented.
Call emergency services if the seizure lasts more than 5 minutes, repeats, or if this is their first seizure.

title: Cardiac Arrest
summary: Cardiac arrest is a medical emergency where the heart stops beating, requiring immediate CPR and emergency help.
steps: Check for responsiveness and normal breathing.
Call emergency services immediately or have someone else call.
Begin chest compressions right away, pushing hard and fast in the center of the chest.
Ask if anyone nearby has access to an AED (automated external defibrillator) and use it if available, following its voice prompts.
Continue CPR without stopping until emergency responders arrive or the person recovers.
Switch with another rescuer every 2 minutes if possible to avoid fatigue and maintain quality compressions.

title: Fractures
summary: A suspected fracture should be kept still and supported to prevent further injury until medical help arrives.
steps: Keep the injured area still and avoid moving the person unless necessary.
Call emergency services for severe, open, or suspected spinal fractures.
Support the injured limb above and below the injury site with your hands.
Apply a splint or padded support if you are trained and help is delayed, without forcing the limb straight.
Apply a cold pack wrapped in cloth to reduce swelling and pain.
Check for signs of shock and keep the person warm and calm.
Do not give the person food or drink in case surgery is needed.
